task.name: Measure how often dev resolves an advisory plan-review finding, so the approve-with-findings policy can be decided on evidence
task.story_text:
## Problem

Plan review approves a plan while holding unresolved P1-level findings, and
passes those findings to dev as advisory context rather than regenerating the
plan. That is a deliberate policy: iterating plans to zero P1s was found to
over-prescribe and box dev in, and the plan phase itself failed often enough that
extra rounds were a poor trade.

The policy has never been evaluated against outcomes, because when it was set
there was no way to observe them. A census of every run that recorded a plan
review — nine in this repository, three in the `hdp` adopter — shows twelve
approvals, zero regenerations, and eleven approvals carrying at least one P1-level
finding. That tells us the policy is operating exactly as designed. It tells us
nothing about whether it is the cheaper choice.

The question turns on a single unmeasured quantity: **how often does dev resolve
an advisory plan finding it was handed?** If that rate is high, the policy is
plainly correct and an extra plan round would be waste on eleven runs out of
twelve. If it is low, each escape is paid for much later and at much higher cost.

There is one known escape, and its shape is why this is worth measuring. The plan
review for `issue-2050` raised a P1-impl describing the defect that later shipped
as #2077 — that the protocol defined a request/response channel but not how the
agent blocks between writing a request and reading a response, so an agent that
writes and continues reads a missing or stale response — and supplied the remedy.
Dev received it as advisory context. The story shipped without it. The defect was
rediscovered when an adopter story produced no work at all, and cost roughly $4.43
directly across the wasted run and two fix stories, plus an investigation and two
days during which the adopter could not use the capability the story existed to
provide.

That is one data point, selected precisely because it was expensive, and it should
not be generalised from. The rest of the eleven findings were largely about module
placement and scope, which dev appears to handle well. Which is the point: the
classes are not alike, and no one currently knows their rates.

The observability needed to answer this landed recently — run provenance and
per-review commit and gate state are now recorded — so plan findings can be joined
to what was actually built. This is measurable now in a way it was not when the
policy was chosen.

## Acceptance criteria

- A resolution rate is produced over a corpus of completed runs: for each recorded
  plan-review finding, whether the change that shipped addressed it.
- The rate is broken out by finding class, because the classes plausibly behave
  differently — a finding about which module owns a step is not the same kind of
  claim as a finding that a mechanism the plan relies on is unspecified.
- Resolved and unresolved findings are both enumerable, so individual escapes can
  be inspected rather than only counted.
- Cost is reported alongside: plan-review phase cost as a fraction of the story it
  guarded, so the marginal cost of an additional plan round is expressed against
  what it protects.
- The result is sufficient to choose between keeping advisory-only, amending plans
  for selected finding classes, and carrying unresolved plan findings forward into
  review, without a further round of analysis.

## Example

A shape sufficient to decide on:

```
Plan advisory resolution — 47 runs, 88 findings

class                        findings  resolved  escaped   rate
module/placement                   34        32        2    94%
scope / out-of-scope               21        20        1    95%
unspecified mechanism              14         8        6    57%
factual error in rationale         12        11        1    92%
already-implemented                 7         6        1    86%

plan review cost:  median $1.50/story   median 3.7% of story cost
escapes by later detection point:
  own code review 5 · own gate 3 · adopter run 2 · unshipped 1

escaped findings:
  issue-2050  unspecified mechanism  -> shipped as #2077  (adopter run)
  issue-1937  already-implemented    -> story rebuilt existing work
  ...
```

The `unspecified mechanism` row is the one the decision hinges on. If it is an
outlier against the others, the policy question is not "more plan rounds or fewer"
but "which finding class justifies one."

## Notes

Deliberately scoped to measurement, not to a policy change. The point is to
replace an instinct with a number; what to do about the number is a separate
decision this issue does not pre-empt.

handoff.summary: Added src/theforge/plan_advisory/ — a read-only measurement of how often dev resolves an advisory plan-review finding. analysis.py is pure extraction/aggregation over audit records (P1-level plan_finding_registry entries on DONE runs, keyed by run_id:ordinal:sha256(normalized description)[:8], plus plan_review.cost_usd / cost.total_usd); report.py loads the substrate via open_readonly and renders; judgments.json is a checked-in corpus of 104 hand-authored judgments supplying finding class and shipped-addressed status, each citing a commit, code site, or the run's own dev handoff notes. Coverage validation is one-directional: a judgment naming no carried finding is fatal, an unjudged audit finding is counted and excluded from rate denominators. Findings whose registry disposition is 'fixed' were resolved by plan regeneration before dev and are split out mechanically. Exposed as a thin 'forge audits plan-advisory' subcommand and recorded in docs/plans/2112-plan-advisory-resolution.md. Result: 29 runs, 104 advisory findings, 96% resolved, four escapes (two still latent), plan review a median 24% of story cost.

commits.message: feat(audits): measure how often dev resolves an advisory plan-review finding

acceptance_criteria.criterion: A resolution rate is produced over a corpus of completed runs: for each recorded plan-review finding, whether the change that shipped addressed it.
acceptance_criteria.notes: 100/104 (96%) over 29 DONE runs. Each judgment records both advisory_outcome (did dev resolve it) and shipped_addressed (did the eventual change carry the remedy), rendered separately.

acceptance_criteria.criterion: The rate is broken out by finding class, because the classes plausibly behave differently.
acceptance_criteria.notes: Eight-class controlled vocabulary seeded from the spec's five, extended with missing failure mode / contract-interface mismatch / test strategy gap where inspected findings genuinely did not fit. Per-class findings/resolved/escaped/rate table.

acceptance_criteria.criterion: Resolved and unresolved findings are both enumerable, so individual escapes can be inspected rather than only counted.
acceptance_criteria.notes: Both lists render with run/issue/class/detection point; --verbose adds each finding's full text and its judgment's evidence.

acceptance_criteria.criterion: Cost is reported alongside: plan-review phase cost as a fraction of the story it guarded.
acceptance_criteria.notes: Median $4.97/story (n=18) and median 24% of story cost (n=17). The 11 runs with no plan-review cost and 12 with no story total are counted and omitted, never imputed.

acceptance_criteria.criterion: The result is sufficient to choose between keeping advisory-only, amending plans for selected finding classes, and carrying unresolved plan findings forward into review, without a further round of analysis.
acceptance_criteria.notes: The doc argues all three against the evidence: advisory-only is favoured (96% at a median 24% plan cost); class amendment has no candidate (unspecified mechanism is 95%, inside the spread). Carrying findings into review is identified as the option the escapes point at and the one this measurement explicitly cannot decide, with the measurement that would decide it named.

story_deviations: The spec's census (9 runs, 11 findings, twelve approvals, zero regenerations) is stale. The substrate holds 29 DONE runs with 119 P1-level plan findings, and plan regeneration does occur — 15 findings were resolved by a regenerated plan before dev. Rather than measure a stale corpus, the analyzer splits fixed-in-plan findings out of the rate mechanically and the doc corrects the census.

The plan reviewer's P1 on corpus bound was taken as option (b): full extraction plus an explicit unjudged bucket, with judged-vs-extracted counts always rendered. In practice all 104 carried findings were judged with citable evidence, so coverage is 100% and the bucket is empty; the machinery remains for when the substrate outgrows the corpus.
The plan reviewer's P2 on DONE-only selection is addressed: 8 excluded runs carrying 29 P1-level findings are counted, enumerated in the report, and named as a selection bias in the doc.
deferred_items: The hdp adopter's three plan-review runs are not reachable from this workspace and are in no count here; stated in both the corpus notes and the doc.
issue-2284 and issue-2347 escapes are still latent defects found by this analysis. Not fixed here (this story is scoped to measurement); both are described precisely enough in the doc to file.

handoff.summary: Iteration 2 advisory cleanup on top of 607a37be. Both P2s were in src/theforge/plan_advisory/report.py. (1) An unusable judgment corpus reached the operator as a traceback. The reviewer cited the missing-'judgments'-list case, but the same escape covered two more shapes: json.JSONDecodeError subclasses ValueError so corrupt JSON took the same path, and a missing file raised OSError, which neither entry point caught. Added _read_corpus(), a single seam that converts OSError and ValueError into CorpusMismatchError, so both `forge audits plan-advisory` and `python -m theforge.plan_advisory` report cleanly without either growing its own except clause. CorpusMismatchError's docstring was widened to state it now covers 'unreadable OR at odds with the substrate' — deliberately one signal, since an operator cannot act differently on the two — and both entry-point messages were reworded to 'judgment corpus unusable'. load_judgments keeps raising ValueError/OSError; it is the low-level reader and its contract is unchanged. (2) Reworded load_report's 'Opens read-only only.' docstring and documented which exceptions it raises. No behaviour change to the measurement itself: the report still renders 29 runs, 104 findings, 96% resolved, 4 escapes.

plan_review.findings:
- [P1-impl] [anthropic-opus-cli] The plan is scoped to the spec's stated census (nine local runs, eleven findings), but the actual substrate is far larger: of 254 records in .forge/audits/runs/, 86 have outcome.final_phase == DONE with a plan_review block, carrying 175 plan_finding_registry entries of which 119 have effective_severity/severity starting with P1. Step 2 requires one hand-authored judgment per extracted P1 finding — each needing diff, review, gate and adopter-evidence inspection — and Step 1 states the analysis 'must fail loudly if ... an audit finding lacks a judgment'. That combination means the story either does not complete or the corpus gets filled with unevidenced judgments, and every AC that rests on the resolution rate goes with it. The plan states no corpus bound (no date window, no cap, no per-class sampling) and no representation for a finding that was extracted but not yet judged.
  Suggestion: Decide the corpus bound in the plan: either (a) restrict extraction to an explicit, stated window or run set sized to what one run can genuinely judge (e.g. the most recent N DONE runs) and report the excluded remainder in corpus metadata, or (b) keep full extraction but add an explicit 'unjudged' bucket — coverage validation then fails only on judgments with no matching audit finding, while unjudged findings are counted and excluded from rate denominators with the count rendered. Either way the report must state judged-vs-extracted counts so the rate is not read as covering the whole corpus.
- [P1-impl] [anthropic-opus-cli] Carried risk: 'Finding classification and resolution require judgment from diffs and review/gate evidence rather than a mechanical audit field.' The stated mitigation is a reviewed JSON corpus validated for exact coverage against audit records — but exact-coverage validation only checks that rows exist, not that any evidence behind them is real, and at 119 findings it is the pressure that turns judgment into guesswork. Confirmed against the substrate: plan_finding_registry entries carry only description, severity, original_severity, effective_severity, cycle_first_seen, cycle_last_seen, disposition — there is no shipped-addressed signal to cross-check a judgment against.
  Suggestion: Require each judgment row to carry a concrete evidence citation (commit sha, review finding id, gate record, or an explicit 'evidence unavailable' marker), and have the analyzer surface a count of judgments whose evidence field is the unavailable marker so an under-evidenced corpus is visible in the rendered report rather than silently averaged in.
- [P2] [anthropic-opus-cli] Step 1 selects on outcome.final_phase == DONE, which drops runs that reached dev and shipped a diff but ended MERGE_FAILED or ESCALATE. Several such records exist with populated plan_finding_registry (e.g. 12ea6040f861.json, 325176a688bc.json, 01ab53ad2f08.json). A plan finding escaping into a run that then escalated is exactly the expensive class the spec cares about.
  Suggestion: State the DONE-only choice explicitly in corpus metadata and the measurement doc, and report how many plan-review-bearing runs were excluded by final_phase so the selection bias is visible; optionally include non-DONE runs in the enumerable escape list even if excluded from the rate.

finding_registry.description: When the judgment corpus JSON file is malformed (e.g., missing "judgments" list), load_judgments raises ValueError, which is not caught by the CLI's exception handler, resulting in an unhandled traceback instead of a clean error message.
The docstring for load_report contains awkward phrasing "Opens read-only only."

soft: Coordinator is pure Python — no LLM calls for routing or process decisions
Schema validation is the integrity boundary — do not relax cross-validation rules

Keep modules single-purpose. Extract when a responsibility separates from its neighbours — never to satisfy a line count. Putting a change in an already-large module is correct if that is where it belongs; a module carved at whatever line got the count down is worse than the large module it came from.
Keep pure-data types in low-dependency modules with stdlib-only imports
Separate prompt construction, output parsing, and coordinator control flow

When adding or modifying data that flows between coordinator phases, instrument the change so the actual values are visible in the audit trail — diagnosing sprint failures requires tracing real data, not reconstructing it
Do not create files outside src/, tests/, or docs/. If you need a scratch file for exploration, delete it before committing.

Changes that affect coordinator phase boundaries, state handoff between phases, or adaptive routing/config propagation must include seam-level integration tests covering the touched boundary. Unit tests alone are insufficient when correctness depends on cross-phase state flow.
